Verbatim match, including the accented examples. Surrounding text: p. 3 'Conventions: Orthographic' adds 'The falling tone is written < ´ >' and the recorded passage is marked '(tone not marked)'; nothing further on stress anywhere in the shee…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gimi is described as having a word-level tone contrast (level vs falling tone on the final vowel of the word); stress is not independent of pitch but is reported to fall on the first syllable of the word that carries high pitch, i.e. it is pitch-conditioned rather than positionally fixed. Scott 1978:22 fn. 32 likewise reports (second-hand, from McBride & McBride 1973:15b) that Gimi is 'recorded as tonal'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the statement is hedged ('tends to') and the data sheet is marked 'partly checked' and 'Draft (posted as is without peer review)'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (OPD lists tone on 'the final vowel' of the word and stress by syllable within the word); examples are isolated citation forms; no phrase-level statement.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD covers Gimi [gim] of Okapa district (villages Agipu, Urap, Negebi, Ubai), i.e. gimi1243 as a whole, with no dialect named. Haiman 1980 (not opened) describes the Zavina dialect (Zavina village) specifically; Glottolog lists no separate glottocode for Zavina. Glottolog's 'Wendy McBride' appears to be an error for Nancy McBride (Scott 1978:205 and the OPD bibliography).

new_statements.relation_note: The only stress statement anywhere on the SIL gim listing is the Organised Phonology Data (entry 42483), which is the very document already quoted in existing_statements; the quote was re-verified verbatim from the native text of the on-disk PDF (p. 2), and the orthographic note on p. 3 (acute = falling tone) is a small addition. The 'grammar file' the tag hoped would state stress is McBride & McBride 1973 'Gimi Grammar Essentials' (entry 58630, 144 pp., Internet Archive copy of the SIL PDF, no text, scanned at 150 dpi covers all 144 pages): it is a tagmemic morphosyntax (Introduction, Morphophonemic note, Words, Phrases, Clauses, Sentences, Sequence of Sentences, Unresolved Issues, Abbrevi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Gimi has a two-way tone contrast (level vs falling) restricted to the final vowel of the word; stress is not independent of pitch: it tends to fall on the first syllable that carries high pitch, so it is derivative of the tonal/pitch pattern rather than a separately assigned or contrastive word-level property. The acute in the orthography marks falling tone, not stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any document on the listing.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the statement is hedged ('tends to occur'). The OPD is a 3-page draft marked 'partly checked' and posted without peer review.
new_statements.identity_note: All material is for Gimi of the Eastern Highlands (Okapa District; ISO gim = gimi1243), not Gimi [gip] of West New Britain. McBride & McBride 1973 (p. 1) explicitly describe 'the southern dialect of the Gimi language.. approximately 10,000 people.. Okapa Sub District', with most fieldwork in the Ubai area; the OPD lists the villages Agipu, Urap, Negebi and Ubai, so both documents describe the same southern (Ubai-area) variety.

sources.note: Family-level only, p. 477: 'In their phonologies, the East-Central Family languages show a strong development of supra-segmental features manifesting themselves in tonal systems and combined tone-stress systems. The glottal stop phoneme appears with extremely high statistical frequency in the languages of the Gahuku and the Kamano Sub-Families, and in Gimi.' Nothing Gimi-specific on stress placement.
